title: Vector & Tensor Analysis
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Vector and Tensor Analysis curriculum: vector algebra (dot/cross/scalar triple products), vector differentiation, gradient/divergence/curl, line/surface/volume integrals, Green's/Stokes'/Gauss divergence theorems, curvilinear coordinates, and an introduction to tensor notation, tensor algebra, the metric tensor, and Christoffel symbols.

questions.question: For vectors A = (1,2,3) and B = (4,5,6), the dot product A·B equals:
The cross product A × B of two vectors is:
options: a vector perpendicular to both A and B
questions.correct_answer: a vector perpendicular to both A and B
questions.explanation: The cross product yields a vector orthogonal to the plane containing A and B, with magnitude |A||B|sinθ.

questions.question: For unit vectors, i × j equals:
questions.correct_answer: k
questions.explanation: By the right-hand rule in a standard Cartesian frame, i × j = k.

questions.question: The scalar triple product A·(B×C) geometrically represents:
options: the volume of the parallelepiped formed by A, B, and C
the area of the parallelogram formed by A and B
the angle between A and B
the projection of A onto B
questions.correct_answer: the volume of the parallelepiped formed by A, B, and C
questions.explanation: The scalar triple product A·(B×C) gives (up to sign) the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the three vectors.

questions.question: If A·(B×C) = 0 for nonzero vectors A, B, C, then A, B, and C are:
questions.correct_answer: coplanar
questions.explanation: A zero scalar triple product means the parallelepiped has zero volume, so the three vectors lie in the same plane.

questions.question: For a scalar field φ(x,y,z), the gradient ∇φ is a:
options: vector field pointing in the direction of steepest increase of φ
scalar equal to the maximum value of φ
vector field with zero divergence always
questions.correct_answer: vector field pointing in the direction of steepest increase of φ
questions.explanation: The gradient of a scalar field is a vector field whose direction gives the direction of maximum rate of increase and whose magnitude gives that rate.

questions.question: For φ = x^2y + z^3, the gradient ∇φ is:
The divergence of a vector field F, div F = ∇·F, measures:
options: the net outward flux per unit volume at a point
the rotational tendency of the field
questions.correct_answer: the net outward flux per unit volume at a point
questions.explanation: Divergence quantifies the net rate of flux (source or sink strength) of a vector field diverging from a point per unit volume.

questions.question: For F = (x^2, y^2, z^2), the divergence ∇·F equals:
The curl of a vector field, curl F = ∇×F, measures:
options: the rotational tendency (circulation density) of the field
the total flux out of a surface
the scalar magnitude of the field
questions.correct_answer: the rotational tendency (circulation density) of the field
questions.explanation: Curl measures the infinitesimal rotation or circulation of a vector field around a point.

questions.question: A vector field F is said to be irrotational if:
questions.explanation: A field with zero curl everywhere is called irrotational; such a field can be expressed as the gradient of a scalar potential.

questions.question: A vector field F is said to be solenoidal if:
questions.explanation: A solenoidal field has zero divergence everywhere, meaning it has no sources or sinks.

questions.question: The identity ∇×(∇φ) for any scalar field φ with continuous second partial derivatives equals:
questions.explanation: The curl of any gradient field is identically zero, a standard vector calculus identity (assuming smoothness).

questions.question: A line integral of a vector field F along a curve C, ∫C F·dr, physically represents:
options: the work done by F along the path C
questions.correct_answer: the work done by F along the path C
questions.explanation: When F represents a force field, ∫C F·dr computes the work done moving a particle along the path C.

questions.question: A line integral of a conservative vector field between two points is:
options: dependent only on the path length
questions.correct_answer: independent of the path taken
questions.explanation: For a conservative field (F = ∇φ), the line integral depends only on the endpoints, not the specific path.

questions.question: A surface integral ∬S F·dS computes:
options: the flux of F through the surface S
the circulation of F around S
the divergence at a point on S
questions.correct_answer: the flux of F through the surface S
questions.explanation: The surface integral of a vector field's dot product with the outward unit normal gives the total flux through the surface.

questions.question: Green's Theorem relates a line integral around a simple closed curve C to:
options: a double integral over the plane region enclosed by C
a triple integral over a volume
a surface integral over a sphere
a single integral along the x-axis
questions.correct_answer: a double integral over the plane region enclosed by C
questions.explanation: Green's theorem converts a line integral around a closed curve in the plane into a double integral over the enclosed region.

questions.question: Stokes' Theorem relates the surface integral of the curl of F over a surface S to:
options: the line integral of F around the boundary curve of S
the divergence integral over the volume bounded by S
the flux of F through a different surface
questions.correct_answer: the line integral of F around the boundary curve of S
questions.explanation: Stokes' theorem states ∬S (∇×F)·dS = ∮C F·dr, where C is the boundary of S.

questions.question: The Gauss Divergence Theorem relates the flux of F through a closed surface S to:
options: the volume integral of ∇·F over the region V enclosed by S
the line integral of F around S
the curl of F at the centroid
questions.correct_answer: the volume integral of ∇·F over the region V enclosed by S
questions.explanation: The divergence theorem states ∬S F·dS = ∭V (∇·F) dV, converting a surface flux integral into a volume integral.

questions.question: In cylindrical coordinates (ρ, φ, z), the volume element dV is:
questions.correct_answer: ρ dρ dφ dz
questions.explanation: The Jacobian for cylindrical coordinates introduces a factor of ρ, giving dV = ρ dρ dφ dz.

questions.question: In spherical coordinates (r, θ, φ), the volume element dV is:
questions.correct_answer: r^2 sinθ dr dθ dφ
questions.explanation: The Jacobian of the spherical coordinate transformation gives dV = r^2 sinθ dr dθ dφ.

questions.question: An orthogonal curvilinear coordinate system is one in which:
options: the coordinate surfaces intersect at right angles everywhere
the scale factors are all equal to 1
questions.correct_answer: the coordinate surfaces intersect at right angles everywhere
questions.explanation: In an orthogonal curvilinear system, the three families of coordinate surfaces are mutually perpendicular at every point.

questions.question: In tensor notation, a quantity with two lower indices, such as A_ij, is called a tensor of:
questions.correct_answer: rank (order) 2, covariant type
questions.explanation: Two subscript (lower) indices indicate a rank-2 covariant tensor; a rank-2 contravariant tensor would carry superscript indices, A^ij.

questions.question: The Kronecker delta δ_ij is defined as:
options: 1 if i = j, and 0 if i ≠ j
0 if i = j, and 1 if i ≠ j
questions.correct_answer: 1 if i = j, and 0 if i ≠ j
questions.explanation: The Kronecker delta is the identity tensor component, equal to 1 for matching indices and 0 otherwise.

questions.question: Under the Einstein summation convention, the expression a_i b^i implies:
options: summation over the repeated index i
summation over all indices except i
questions.correct_answer: summation over the repeated index i
questions.explanation: Einstein's summation convention states that a repeated index (once as subscript, once as superscript) implies summation over that index.

questions.question: A contravariant vector A^i transforms under a coordinate change x^i → x'^i according to:
questions.correct_answer: A'^i = (∂x'^i/∂x^j) A^j
questions.explanation: Contravariant components transform using the Jacobian of the new coordinates with respect to the old, ∂x'^i/∂x^j.

questions.question: A covariant vector A_i transforms under a coordinate change x^i → x'^i according to:
questions.correct_answer: A'_i = (∂x^j/∂x'^i) A_j
questions.explanation: Covariant components transform with the inverse Jacobian, ∂x^j/∂x'^i, opposite to contravariant components.

questions.question: The operation of contraction in tensor algebra involves:
options: setting one upper and one lower index equal and summing
adding two tensors of the same rank
multiplying a tensor by a scalar
raising every index of a tensor
questions.correct_answer: setting one upper and one lower index equal and summing
questions.explanation: Contraction reduces the rank of a tensor by two, by equating one contravariant and one covariant index and summing over it.

questions.question: Two tensors can only be added or subtracted if they:
options: have the same rank and the same index structure (type)
questions.correct_answer: have the same rank and the same index structure (type)
questions.explanation: Tensor addition requires matching rank and matching arrangement of covariant/contravariant indices, so the result transforms consistently.

questions.question: The metric tensor g_ij is used primarily to:
options: define distances (line element) and raise/lower tensor indices
compute the determinant of a matrix
questions.correct_answer: define distances (line element) and raise/lower tensor indices
questions.explanation: The metric tensor determines the line element ds^2 = g_ij dx^i dx^j and is used to convert between covariant and contravariant components.

questions.question: In ordinary flat Euclidean space using Cartesian coordinates, the metric tensor g_ij equals:
options: a tensor with all entries equal to 1
questions.correct_answer: the Kronecker delta δ_ij
questions.explanation: In Cartesian coordinates on flat space, the metric reduces to the identity, g_ij = δ_ij, since ds^2 = dx^2+dy^2+dz^2.

questions.question: The Christoffel symbols Γ^k_ij arise when differentiating tensor components in curvilinear coordinates because:
options: the basis vectors themselves change from point to point
the metric tensor is always constant
questions.correct_answer: the basis vectors themselves change from point to point
questions.explanation: In curvilinear coordinates, basis vectors vary in direction/magnitude across space, and the Christoffel symbols account for this variation in the covariant derivative.
